speaker: Andrej Karpathy
title: Skill Issue: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents, AutoResearch, and the Loopy Era of AI
question: In machine learning research, what makes it possible for an open pool of untrusted contributors on the internet to safely collaborate on improving models?
guest: In model optimization, you're trying to find code that trains a model to a very low validation loss. If someone from the internet gives you a candidate commit claiming better performance, they could lie, so you have to check it yourself. It looks a bit like a blockchain where instead of blocks you have commits building on each other, and the proof of work is doing tons of experimentation to find the few commits that work. Fundamentally, a huge amount of search goes into trying thousands of failed ideas, but it is very cheap to verify a candidate solution because you only have to run a single training check. Long story short, you pair an asynchronous untrusted pool of workers doing search with a trusted pool of workers doing verification—while sandboxing security carefully since running arbitrary submitted code is risky. Just like Folding@home, it works because solutions are very expensive to discover but very cheap to verify.

points.core: Discovering an improved training change requires vastly more compute than verifying one.
points.note: Accept: search-verification asymmetry, trying thousands of failed experiments versus running a single validation check, or hard-to-find/cheap-to-verify structure (e.g., Folding@home). Do not credit: generic claims that crowdsourcing adds more compute or more ideas.

points.core: A smaller trusted pool must independently re-run submitted commits to block dishonest claims.
points.note: Accept: separating untrusted search workers from trusted verifiers who re-evaluate candidate solutions against an objective metric like validation loss. Do not credit: relying on reputation, peer review, or assuming contributors are honest.

points.core: Verifiers must sandbox untrusted code execution because arbitrary submitted scripts pose security risks.
points.note: Accept: isolating or sandboxing external code submissions to prevent malicious execution on verification hardware. Do not credit: generic mentions of security or safety without tying it to executing arbitrary untrusted code.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The key enabler is cheap, objective verification: finding an improvement is expensive, but checking one is easy. This answer is from memory rather than a web search.

If a contributor proposes a change (a code commit, a hyperparameter setting, a training trick or a model update), a trusted party can re-run it against a fixed metric, such as validation loss on held-out data under a fixed compute budget. It then accepts the change only if the result reproduces. No trust in the contributor is needed, because bad or malicious submissions simply fail the check. This is the asymmetry Andrej Karpathy has pointed to for "autoresearch"-style open collaboration, comparing it to proof-of-work, where a huge untrusted search effort is filtered by a small trusted verification effort.

Two caveats apply. Submitted code must be run in a sandbox, since it is untrusted. And where contributors send gradients or weights rather than verifiable experiments, as in federated or volunteer-compute training, safety instead relies on Byzantine-robust aggregation, secure aggregation and validation of updates.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Safe collaboration among untrusted internet contributors relies on replacing trust in participants with independent, reproducible verification and strict separation between proposing changes and evaluating them. Because searching for improvements is computationally expensive while testing a promising candidate is comparatively cheap, open projects let anyone experiment freely while gating acceptance through a trusted, tamper-proof evaluation harness.

In algorithmic and automated research, contributors submit small, auditable code diffs rather than opaque model weights or self-reported scores. Sandboxed execution restricts edit scope so submissions cannot alter data loaders, timers, or scoring logic, and an independent verifier reproduces runs under fixed compute budgets against held-out validation data before merging gains. When contributors instead supply distributed training compute, gradients, or rollouts, protocols combine reproducible spot-check recomputation to catch fabricated work, Byzantine-resilient aggregation to filter poisoned or outlier updates, and validation-gated checkpoints. Together, sandboxing, held-out benchmarks, and cheap verification ensure that noisy or malicious contributions are discarded while genuine improvements safely compound.

noweb.answer:
Open collaboration among untrusted contributors relies on replacing interpersonal trust with automated verification, fault-tolerant aggregation, and strict software boundaries. The primary enabler is verification asymmetry: although computing gradients or generating training data is expensive, peers or coordinators can cheaply audit contributions by deterministically recomputing small random subsets of training steps and evaluating candidate updates against private, held-out benchmarks.

To neutralize subtle data poisoning, backdoors, or faulty hardware that slip past spot checks, distributed training protocols apply Byzantine-resilient aggregation—such as geometric medians, trimmed means, and strict norm clipping—which bounds how much any single participant can shift the shared weights. At the systems layer, tensor-only serialization formats like Safetensors replace executable formats like pickle, while sandboxed runtimes isolate untrusted scripts so shared artifacts cannot run arbitrary code on collaborators' machines. Combined with cryptographic provenance and reputation or stake-slashing incentives that penalize dishonest nodes, these mechanisms ensure that malicious or defective contributions are filtered out before they can compromise host infrastructure or model quality.

Peer or coordinator spot checks and held-out evaluations do not establish that a separate trusted pool independently reruns submitted commits.
The response explicitly connects sandboxing untrusted scripts with preventing arbitrary code execution on collaborators’ machines.

What makes it work is an asymmetry. Finding an improvement is expensive, but checking one is cheap. This idea is most closely tied to Andrej Karpathy's "autoresearch" proposal from 2026, as I recall it; I didn't look up the source for this answer.

The setup has a fixed, objective benchmark: for example, train for a set compute or time budget and measure validation loss (bits per byte) on held-out data. Contributors, whether people or AI agents, may spend a lot of compute exploring ideas. Each one submits a concrete change, such as a code commit, a configuration or a set of weights. Anyone can rerun it and confirm that the metric really improved. Because a single rerun checks a claim, you don't need to trust the contributor's honesty, skill or motives. Bad, fake or malicious submissions fail the check and get thrown out. Verified improvements are merged and become the new baseline for the next round.

This works much like proof-of-work in blockchains or volunteer computing projects such as SETI@home. Trust comes from cheap, reproducible verification against a fixed, hard-to-game metric, not from knowing who the contributors are. That only holds if the evaluation is deterministic, reproducible and protected from tampering or overfitting.

models.answer: Safe collaboration among an open pool of untrusted contributors relies primarily on asymmetric, objective verification: discovering a genuine model improvement is computationally expensive, whereas checking whether a proposed change actually works is relatively cheap. In practice, untrusted participants—whether humans or autonomous research agents—explore freely and submit candidate improvements such as compact code diffs, hyperparameter changes, or model updates, while a smaller trusted pool of verifiers independently reproduces and evaluates them. Because submitted code is executed inside isolated sandboxes and scored against fixed, held-out benchmarks rather than self-reported metrics, malicious code, data poisoning, and reward hacking can be filtered out automatically. In decentralized training settings where contributors share gradients directly, Byzantine-robust aggregation and cryptographic or consensus-based proofs serve the same gatekeeping role. Only submissions that verifiably beat the current baseline are committed to the canonical model state, creating a tamper-resistant progression—much like a versioned ledger—that lets anyone build on the latest checkpoint without ever needing to trust other contributors.

noweb.answer: Safe collaboration among untrusted contributors relies on combining objective verification, robust aggregation, and influence-bounding mechanisms. First, contributions—whether gradients, datasets, or fine-tuned checkpoints—are evaluated against trusted, held-out validation benchmarks and automated safety checks before being merged, ensuring that degraded or backdoored updates are rejected. When participants submit gradients during distributed or federated training, Byzantine-robust aggregation rules such as coordinate-wise medians, trimmed means, or distance-based filtering (like Krum) prevent a minority of malicious actors from poisoning or diverging the model. Gradient clipping and anomaly detection further bound the influence any single contributor can exert. To deter Sybil attacks and fabricated work, decentralized protocols can also incorporate cryptographic verification of computation, redundant cross-checking by peers, and reputation or economic staking systems. Together, these defenses shift trust away from individual contributors and onto mathematical guarantees, empirical validation, and verifiable incentives.

noweb.answer: An open pool of contributors can improve a model when anyone can propose a change and maintainers can independently verify it before adoption. Contributors submit code or model updates to an isolated evaluation environment. The project checks each candidate against the current model using private held-out data, regression tests, and checks for behaviors such as backdoors. Only candidates that meet the acceptance criteria are merged, and versioning makes it possible to trace and roll back changes. The system relies on trusted evaluation and controlled integration, so contributors can participate without having direct access to the shared model.

models.answer: An open pool of untrusted contributors can improve a shared model when anyone can propose an update, but each update must earn acceptance. Contributors can train locally and submit candidate changes. A separate evaluation process tests whether a change improves the current model on held-out tasks and checks for regressions or harmful behavior before merging it. Sandboxing limits what submitted code can do, and versioning lets maintainers roll back a change if problems emerge later. This lets the project rely on evidence about each contribution instead of the contributor’s reputation, though no finite set of tests can rule out every hidden failure.
